Card text: Need better contact data
Problem statement: Missing or wrong emails, phone numbers, and job titles make it hard to reach the right people.
How this agent solves it: Each contact gets a field-by-field check of email, phone and title, with source and date, and anything it can't confirm is marked unknown so reps know what to verify.
Ask them about this problem: Which is wrong or missing most often for you: emails, phone numbers or titles?
What the agent does: Checks contacts before anyone reaches out, finds missing or out-of-date emails, phone numbers, job titles and employers, and proposes corrections with a source for each, so reps reach the right people.
How it works: A rep uploads a prospect list, or a weekly check runs on CRM contacts (to confirm) → the agent compares each person's title and employer with public profiles, company team pages and announcements, and checks that each email domain can receive mail → it marks every field confirmed, changed or unknown, with the source and date → an ops owner reviews the proposed corrections before anything is written back to the CRM.
Data it uses: Public profiles, company team pages, announcements and email domain records; CRM contacts, bounce history from the sending tool, and any data vendor or email checker already in use (to confirm).
Who uses it: RevOps owns the checks and approves CRM updates; SDRs and AEs get corrected lists before outreach starts; CSMs hear when a client contact has moved.
First version: Check one rep's next 200 prospects plus last month's bounced emails, marking each field confirmed, changed or unknown, and compare the results with what the rep finds by hand.
How we'd measure it: Bounce rate on checked lists against unchecked ones; share of proposed corrections the ops owner approves unchanged.

Card text: Still guessing which accounts to target
Problem statement: There's no reliable way to tell which companies actually need what we sell.
How this agent solves it: Each account is scored against criteria drawn from your actual wins and losses (to confirm), with the evidence for each point shown, so targeting rests on checkable reasons.
Ask them about this problem: When a deal closed quickly, what was true about that company beforehand?
What the agent does: Turns your best customers into written fit criteria, finds and scores companies that match, fills in missing company facts, and builds one ranked target list that sales and marketing both work from, with the reason behind every score.
How it works: Sales and marketing agree fit criteria, drafted from past wins and losses (to confirm) → the agent finds matching companies on the public web and fills in size, industry, location and other agreed fields → it scores each account, showing which criteria it met, missed or couldn't check, and proposes a priority tier and owner → both teams review one shared list; approved fields go back to the CRM only after sign-off (to confirm).
Data it uses: Past won and lost deals and CRM account fields (to confirm); public company websites, job posts, news and business registries for size, industry and location.
Who uses it: RevOps owns the criteria and the list; sales and marketing leaders agree priority tiers together; SDRs and AEs work the accounts while campaigns target the same list.
First version: A read-only scored list of 200 accounts, half already in the CRM with blank fields and half newly found, reviewed in one session by a sales lead and a marketing lead.
How we'd measure it: Hours spent building lists before and after; share of listed accounts both teams accept; meeting rate on top-tier accounts compared with the rest.

Card text: Too much tab switching for account research
Problem statement: Researching one company means jumping between its website, LinkedIn, the CRM, and other tools.
How this agent solves it: It reads the website, public profiles, news and CRM history (to confirm) in one pass and puts the findings on one page, each line linked to its source.
Ask them about this problem: How long does researching one account take today, and which step takes longest?
What the agent does: Builds a one-page brief on any account before a rep touches it, and refreshes it before each client conversation, so the research happens once, stays current, and lands where the team already works.
How it works: Someone names an account, or a client meeting is booked (calendar to confirm) → the agent reads the company's site, news, job posts and public profiles, plus CRM history and notes (to confirm) → it writes a brief with ICP fit, likely buying roles, recent changes and a suggested angle, each line sourced and dated → before each meeting it re-checks and leads with what changed, in the account record or Slack (to confirm).
Data it uses: Public web, news, job posts and profiles; CRM account and activity history, past meeting notes and calendar (access to confirm).
Who uses it: SDRs and AEs read it before outreach; account leads and partners read the refreshed version before client meetings; the sales manager spot-checks quality.
First version: Briefs for 25 accounts from one rep's list, compared side by side with that rep's own research, plus refreshed briefs for five upcoming client meetings, checked by whoever runs each meeting.
How we'd measure it: Research minutes per account before and after; share of briefs reps rate "usable as is"; client meetings where the brief missed a change the client raised.

Card text: Missing contacts on the buying team
Problem statement: We know one person at the account, but we're missing others involved in choosing a product.
How this agent solves it: Starting from the one contact you know, it finds their manager, peers and the other teams usually involved in choosing a product, each with its source.
Ask them about this problem: How many people end up involved in a typical deal, and how many do you know early?
What the agent does: Maps who is likely involved in a purchase at an account: the team that owns the problem, the people who shape the choice, and who can approve the spend, with the evidence and confidence for each.
How it works: A rep names an account or an open deal → the agent reads public profiles, team pages, job posts and announcements, plus CRM contacts and call notes (to confirm) → it identifies the department that owns the problem you solve and lists likely users, evaluators and approvers, each marked confirmed, inferred or unknown → the rep reviews the map and chooses who to contact; nothing is added to the CRM without approval.
Data it uses: Public profiles, company team pages, job posts and leadership announcements; CRM contacts, call notes and who signed past deals (to confirm).
Who uses it: AEs and SDRs use it on target accounts and open deals; sales managers use it in deal reviews; marketing uses the role list for campaigns aimed at those accounts.
First version: Maps for 15 open deals, checked by each deal owner, plus 10 closed deals to see whether it would have found the person who actually signed.
How we'd measure it: Share of mapped roles reps confirm as correct; deals where the approver was named before the proposal went out.

Card text: Intent isn't intenting
Problem statement: The data says an account is interested, but that interest doesn't turn into a real buying conversation.
How this agent solves it: It treats an intent score as one clue, recommends a call only when fit and a second sign agree, and tracks which combinations of signs actually led to conversations.
Ask them about this problem: Of the accounts your intent data flagged last quarter, how many became real conversations?
What the agent does: Combines intent data, website visits and public buying signals into one short, dated note per account that explains what triggered it, then recommends a play that fits how ready the account looks, so reps see only the few worth acting on now.
How it works: Daily, the agent collects intent alerts, website visits and CRM activity (to confirm), plus public signals like hiring, funding and leadership changes → it groups them by account and checks them against each other and the account's fit → it writes one note per account: what happened, when, what it may mean and what's still unknown → each rep gets a short ranked list with a suggested play: call, send something useful, or wait.
Data it uses: Intent data feeds, website visit data, marketing engagement and CRM activity (all to confirm); public job posts, news, funding announcements and leadership changes.
Who uses it: Marketing ops or RevOps owns the signal rules; SDRs and AEs work the ranked list; marketing handles accounts not yet ready; sales leaders check which signals led to meetings.
First version: Run it on last quarter's intent alerts and website visits to see which accounts it would have ranked highest, and compare them with the accounts that actually opened a deal.
How we'd measure it: Share of recommended calls that become real buying conversations; account alerts each rep receives per week, before and after.

Card text: Gotta be quicker with inbound leads
Problem statement: People ask about our product, but we take too long to get back to them.
How this agent solves it: Research and a draft reply are ready when the request arrives, so the rep only reviews and sends, and leads left waiting past an agreed time are flagged.
Ask them about this problem: How long does a new inbound request usually wait before someone replies, and why?
What the agent does: Gives every inbound lead a fast first reply that fits how they found you: it researches the person, labels the source and request, and drafts a matching response for a rep to approve while the request is still fresh.
How it works: A demo request, form fill, referral or ad response arrives (sources to confirm) → the workflow checks the person and company against public sources and the CRM (to confirm), and labels the source and request → it drafts a reply to match: a booking link for demo requests, a note naming the referrer for referrals, a useful resource for ad responses → the rep approves or edits it, and leads still waiting are flagged.
Data it uses: Form submissions, demo requests, referral notes and ad campaign details, plus CRM records (all to confirm); public company and profile information.
Who uses it: Marketing ops owns the source rules and reply templates; SDRs or AEs approve and send; the sales manager watches response times.
First version: Two weeks on demo requests and referrals only, with every draft approved by a rep and the time to first reply logged for each lead.
How we'd measure it: Time from inbound request to first reply, before and after; meeting rate by lead source.

Card text: Nobody wants to cold call
Problem statement: Calling someone who hasn't asked to hear from us is the task everyone keeps putting off.
How this agent solves it: Each call in a scheduled block comes with a sourced reason the prospect might care now, an opener and objection answers, warmest prospects first.
Ask them about this problem: When a rep skips a call block, what's the usual reason?
What the agent does: Prepares a short call sheet for each prospect in a call block: who they are, why the call is timely, an opener, likely objections with answers, and which number to try, so reps pick up the phone ready.
How it works: A rep schedules a call block → the agent picks best-fit prospects with a recent, sourced reason to call, warmest first, and checks which numbers look current (to confirm) → for each it writes a one-page call sheet: why now, an opener, two questions and answers to likely objections → after each call, the rep's quick notes become a draft follow-up and CRM update to approve (to confirm).
Data it uses: Public news, job posts and profiles; the rep's prospect list, CRM history, phone numbers and past call outcomes (to confirm).
Who uses it: SDRs and AEs use the call sheets; the sales manager schedules call blocks and reviews sheet quality; RevOps confirms where call outcomes are logged.
First version: Call sheets for one rep's next 20 calls in a single call block, with the rep noting which sheets helped and which openers started a real conversation.
How we'd measure it: Calls made per scheduled block before and after; share of calls that become real conversations.

Card text: Event leads go cold before we follow up
Problem statement: By the time we email someone we met at an event, the conversation is no longer fresh.
How this agent solves it: Reps get same-day drafts that mention what was discussed at the booth, so writing no longer delays the first email and the person still remembers the conversation.
Ask them about this problem: What do reps write down after a booth conversation, and where do those notes end up?
What the agent does: Turns a badge scan or booth note into a personal follow-up draft within hours, while the conversation is still remembered.
How it works: At the end of each event day, the attendee list or booth notes arrive → each person is matched to their company and to any existing CRM record (to confirm) → the workflow drafts a follow-up that references what was actually discussed, plus one relevant resource → a rep approves or edits it before anything is sent.
Data it uses: Event attendee export, booth or scanner notes and CRM records (all to confirm); public company context.
Who uses it: Field or event marketing owns it; reps approve and send.
First version: Run it on one event's list, with every draft human-approved.
How we'd measure it: Hours from event to first touch; reply rate against the last comparable event.

Card text: Sales emails that could be for anyone
Problem statement: Adding a first name doesn't make the rest of the email relevant to that person's business.
How this agent solves it: Each email is built around one fact about the prospect's business, such as a new market or a hiring push, and links it to how you help.
Ask them about this problem: Beyond the first name, what does a rep usually change in an email for each prospect?
What the agent does: Drafts a short first email for each prospect around one specific, sourced reason to talk now, written in your team's own voice, for a rep to edit and send.
How it works: A rep picks a prospect, or one arrives from a target list → the agent reads recent company news, job posts, the person's public posts and role, plus CRM history (to confirm), and picks the most timely reason to reach out → it drafts a short email in the style of your best past emails, citing its source → the rep edits and sends; if no good reason exists, the agent says so.
Data it uses: Public news, job posts, company pages and profiles; your best-performing past emails, messaging guide and CRM history (to confirm).
Who uses it: SDRs and AEs edit and send drafts; marketing owns the voice guide and approved claims; sales managers review a sample of drafts each week.
First version: Drafts for 30 prospects on one rep's list, mixed in with that rep's own emails, so the team can judge relevance and try to spot which ones a tool wrote.
How we'd measure it: Minutes to produce a send-ready email; reply rate against the rep's usual emails; share of drafts sent with light edits.

Card text: Great demo. Then we get ghosted.
Problem statement: The demo seems to go well, but the buyer stops replying and there's no agreed next step.
How this agent solves it: After each demo it checks the notes for an agreed, dated next step; if none exists or the buyer goes quiet, the rep gets a recap draft proposing one.
Ask them about this problem: In your last ghosted deal, what had the buyer agreed to do next?
What the agent does: Follows each demo from booking to agreed next step: it drafts reminders tied to what the buyer asked to see, checks whether a next step was agreed, and flags no-shows and buyers who go quiet.
How it works: A demo is booked → the workflow drafts a reminder naming what the buyer asked to see, and flags bookings the buyer hasn't confirmed → after the call, it reads notes or the transcript (to confirm) and records the agreed next step, open questions and who else should join → after a no-show, a missing next step or a quiet week, the rep gets a drafted reschedule note or recap to edit and send.
Data it uses: Calendar bookings and booking-form answers, call notes or transcripts, email reply status and CRM opportunity records (all to confirm); public company context.
Who uses it: Sales or marketing ops owns it; AEs and SDRs edit and send every draft; the sales manager reviews demos left without a next step.
First version: The next 30 demos booked by one team, with every reminder and recap approved by the rep, plus a daily list of demos that ended without a next step.
How we'd measure it: Show rate for booked demos, before and after; share of completed demos that end with a dated next step.

Card text: Our competitor notes are already out of date
Problem statement: The comparison sheet still describes an old version of the other product.
Roles: Sales & prospecting; Marketing & growth; Strategy & market intelligence
How this agent solves it: Each line of the comparison sheet carries a source and date; when a competitor page changes, the agent proposes the edit, and lines past their review date are flagged.
Ask them about this problem: Who owns the comparison sheet today, and when was it last updated?
What the agent does: Watches named competitors' public pages for launches, pricing changes and product updates, keeps the comparison sheet dated and sourced, and checks claims reps hear against public evidence, so the team learns of changes before clients mention them.
How it works: Daily, the agent checks competitors' product, pricing, release-note and news pages → it compares them with the last saved copy and confirms changes with a second source where possible → it writes a note on what changed, with evidence and what it may mean, for reps facing that competitor (to confirm) → it proposes dated edits to the comparison sheet for an owner to approve; reps can also submit claims to check.
Data it uses: Competitor websites, pricing pages, release notes, press, review sites and job posts; CRM deal records naming competitors (to confirm); the current comparison sheet (to confirm).
Who uses it: Product marketing or market intelligence owns it and approves sheet edits; sales leaders review alerts; reps use the sheet and submit claims to check.
First version: Three competitors watched for a month: a weekly digest of verified changes, a comparison sheet with a date and source on each line, and answers to claims reps submit.
How we'd measure it: Competitor changes the team knew about before a client or prospect raised them; share of comparison sheet lines with a recent dated source.

Card text: Hard to check what the AI is doing
Problem statement: We can't easily see the steps an AI tool is taking or the actions it has already carried out.
Roles: Sales & prospecting; Marketing & growth; Customer success & accounts; Revenue & marketing ops; Strategy & market intelligence; Systems & AI; Support & customer experience; Risk, fraud & payments
How this agent solves it: Each run keeps a plain-English step log, with times, of what it searched, read, changed or sent, so anyone can see what it has already done.
Ask them about this problem: When an AI tool acts for you, how do you find out what it actually did?
What the agent does: A standard every agent follows: each answer lists the steps and actions taken, links every fact to the record or page it came from, and marks what is inferred or unknown, so anyone can check it.
How it works: As an agent runs, it logs each step in plain English: searches, records read, actions taken → its answer tags each fact with the link or record ID used, marks what is inferred and lists what is still unknown → a checking pass flags any fact with no source, or a source that does not support it → the answer, step log and sources are saved together for later review.
Data it uses: Each agent's step log and saved answers; the public pages and internal records it reads, such as CRM fields, notes or tickets (access to confirm per system).
Who uses it: GTM Engineering or Business Systems sets the standard and checks new agents against it; anyone reading an answer can check its sources; team leads review flagged answers.
First version: Apply the standard to one agent already in use. Two users check 20 answers each: can they follow the steps, and does every fact have a source that supports it?
How we'd measure it: Share of sampled answers where every fact has a source that supports it; minutes to trace an answer back to its records.

Card text: The AI demo works. The real workflow doesn't.
Problem statement: The demo handles a neat example but fails when real work brings exceptions and messy data.
Roles: Sales & prospecting; Marketing & growth; Customer success & accounts; Revenue & marketing ops; Strategy & market intelligence; Systems & AI; Support & customer experience; Risk, fraud & payments
How this agent solves it: The agent is scored on real past cases, including exceptions and messy data, before launch; each new exception found in live use is added to the set.
Ask them about this problem: What was the first real case that broke the demo, and what made it different?
What the agent does: Tests an AI agent on real, messy past work before launch and after every change. A scorecard agreed before the pilot starts shows accuracy and whether checking the output takes less time than doing the task by hand.
How it works: Before the pilot, the team agrees a baseline and success measures, and saves real past cases, exceptions included, with the accepted answer → every agent change reruns all saved cases and scores them against those answers → reviewers check only cases that failed or changed → in live use, reviewers mark each output used as is, edited or redone, with minutes spent → a weekly scorecard compares accuracy and review time with the baseline.
Data it uses: Real past cases and the answers the team accepted (to confirm); agent outputs; reviewer marks and minutes; time per task done by hand, as the baseline.
Who uses it: The team running the pilot owns the scorecard; GTM Engineering maintains the test cases; reviewers mark each output; a named sponsor decides whether to expand, fix or stop it.
First version: One agent and 50 real past cases, messy ones included. Score the current version, agree the scorecard, then run two weeks with every output reviewed and marked used as is, edited or redone.
How we'd measure it: Review and correction minutes per output against doing the task by hand; share of real cases, exceptions included, the agent gets right.

Card text: Old leads never get a second look
Problem statement: Someone who wasn't ready before may be ready now, but we never revisit the old conversation.
How this agent solves it: It reads each old conversation for the stated reason and timing, such as budget next year, and flags the lead when that reason looks resolved or the date arrives.
Ask them about this problem: What are the usual reasons a lead isn't ready, and how would you know they've changed?
What the agent does: Goes back through old leads and lost conversations, finds the ones where the reason they weren't ready may have changed, and gives the rep a dated reason to reopen, with the old conversation summarized.
How it works: Monthly, the agent reads lost and stalled leads, their emails, notes and loss reasons (to confirm) → it records why each wasn't ready and any date they gave to revisit → it checks public sources for changes since, such as a new leader, funding or hiring → it ranks the few worth reopening now, with dated evidence, what's still unknown and an opener that picks up the old conversation → reps choose which to reopen.

Who uses it: Sales ops or the SDR manager owns it; SDRs and AEs choose which leads to reopen; the sales manager reviews whether revived leads were worth the time.
First version: A one-time review of last year's lost leads for one team: the 25 most promising, each with the old reason and new evidence, checked by the reps who owned them.
How we'd measure it: Reply and meeting rate on reopened leads compared with new cold leads; pipeline created from leads that had been closed or stalled.

Card text: Interested replies stuck in a shared inbox
Problem statement: Positive replies arrive, but nobody takes responsibility for answering them.
How this agent solves it: Each positive reply in the shared inbox is flagged with a proposed owner from account ownership and a deadline, and reminders continue until someone answers it.
Ask them about this problem: Who checks the shared inbox today, and how long does a positive reply usually wait?
What the agent does: Spots interested replies, warm introduction offers and conversations waiting on an absent rep, then proposes who should act on each one and by when, so no hot conversation sits without an owner.
How it works: A message arrives in the shared inbox or a chosen chat channel (to confirm) → it is labeled: interested reply, introduction offer, question, not interested or auto-reply → the workflow proposes an owner from account ownership, or a backup if calendars or out-of-office notes show the owner is away (to confirm) → the owner gets a deadline and reminders until someone answers; a manager approves any reassignment, with no automatic rerouting in version one.
Data it uses: Shared inbox and outreach tool replies, chosen team chat channels, CRM account ownership, rep calendars and out-of-office status (all to confirm).

Card text: Can't find who signs off on the deal

Card text: Client review decks eat up the week
Problem statement: Preparing each customer review means gathering the same information and rebuilding slides by hand.
How this agent solves it: Drafts each review deck on your template from usage, results, tickets and notes, so the CSM checks and edits slides rather than gathering data and rebuilding them by hand.
Ask them about this problem: Which slides in your review deck do you rebuild every time, and from which systems?
What the agent does: Starts each renewal early with a brief and a draft review deck built from the client's own data. The brief names any doubts the client has, with evidence, so the CSM can resolve them before price comes up.
How it works: When a contract end date or notice deadline enters the window the team chooses, the agent gathers usage, results, open tickets, contacts and call notes (sources to confirm) → it writes a renewal brief: value delivered, the client's doubts with evidence, and what's still unknown → it drafts review slides from the same facts → the CSM edits both and decides the renewal approach, including any discount, with their manager.
Data it uses: Contract end dates and notice terms, product usage, support tickets, CRM notes and call transcripts, past review decks and renewal outcomes (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: CS Ops owns the schedule and deck template; CSMs edit and present; the CS manager checks any discount request against the brief.
First version: Briefs and draft decks for the next 10 renewals in one CSM's book, compared with what that CSM would have built by hand and how long it took.
How we'd measure it: Days between the first renewal conversation and the contract end date; share of renewals closed with a discount, before and after.

Card text: Discounting every renewal to keep the client
Problem statement: Price cuts have become the default way to keep clients instead of resolving why they're unsure.
How this agent solves it: Lists why the client is unsure, from calls, tickets and emails, with a non-price response for each, so the CSM can address the cause before offering a price cut.
Ask them about this problem: On your last discounted renewal, what was the client actually unsure about?
What the agent does: Starts each renewal early with a brief and a draft review deck built from the client's own data. The brief names any doubts the client has, with evidence, so the CSM can resolve them before price comes up.

Card text: Renewal paperwork takes too many handoffs
Problem statement: A client is ready to renew, but internal approvals and document handoffs hold up the agreement.
Roles: Customer success & accounts; Revenue & marketing ops
How this agent solves it: For each client ready to renew, names the approval or document holding up the agreement and who has it, and shows which handoffs most often cause delays.
Ask them about this problem: Which approval or handoff most often holds up a renewal, and why?
What the agent does: Tracks each renewal from the client's yes to the signed agreement, showing which approval or document is holding it up, who has it and for how long, so stalled steps get chased early.
How it works: A renewal is marked as agreed in the CRM (to confirm) → the workflow lists the approvals and documents it needs, based on its terms and your approval rules → it checks each step's status daily and records who holds it and since when → the renewal owner gets a daily list of stuck steps; automatic reminders to approvers (to confirm) come only after review.
Data it uses: CRM renewal records and stages, approval records, contract and order form status in the document or e-signature tool, renewal terms such as price changes (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: RevOps or the deal desk owns it; the renewal owner chases stuck steps; approvers see what waits on them; the CS leader reviews where time is lost.
First version: A read-only tracker for this quarter's renewals, checked against what the renewals team believes is holding each one up.
How we'd measure it: Days from the client's yes to the signed agreement; handoffs per renewal, and where the waiting time sits.

Card text: Upsell pitch lands during a support nightmare
Problem statement: We ask a client to buy more while they're still waiting for us to fix a serious problem.
How this agent solves it: Marks accounts with a serious open ticket as "fix first", so anyone planning to ask that client to buy more sees the problem and waits for the fix.
Ask them about this problem: What happened the last time someone pitched more to a client still waiting on a fix?
What the agent does: Matches every support ticket to its client and account owner, ranks open issues by business impact with the reasons shown, and warns sales before anyone pitches a client who is still waiting on a serious fix.
How it works: A support ticket opens or changes → the workflow links it to the client account and owner → it rates impact from severity, users affected, time open, repeat issues and renewal date, and explains why → each account team gets a daily ranked digest of its clients' open issues → accounts with a serious open issue are marked "fix first" in a shared list; CRM write-back (to confirm) only after review.
Data it uses: Support tickets and status, CRM accounts, owners, open opportunities and renewal dates, product usage by account (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: RevOps or Support Ops owns it; CSMs and account managers act on the digest; sales checks the fix-first flag before outreach; the CS leader reviews ratings.
First version: A daily digest for one account team over two weeks, with each impact rating checked against how the CSM would have ranked the same issues.
How we'd measure it: Time from a serious ticket opening to the account owner hearing about it; upsell pitches made while a serious ticket was open.

Card text: Existing clients treated like brand-new leads
Problem statement: Current customers enter prospect campaigns because our systems don't recognize that they already buy from us.
Roles: Customer success & accounts; Revenue & marketing ops
How this agent solves it: It matches every campaign contact against current customer accounts (to confirm) by company domain and name, including client subsidiaries, and flags matches for the account owner before launch.
Ask them about this problem: How does your marketing team know which companies already buy from you?
What the agent does: Checks every outreach list and automated follow-up against declines, opt-outs and current customers before messages go out, and flags anyone who shouldn't be contacted, with the reason, for a person to review.
How it works: A list is imported or an automated follow-up is due to send (tools to confirm) → the workflow checks each person against opt-outs from every tool and current customer accounts → it reads recent replies for clear no's, like 'not interested' or 'please stop', even when nobody marked them → it lists flagged people with the reason; an ops owner reviews, and automatic holds start only once the checks prove accurate.
Data it uses: Outreach and email tool lists, sequences and replies; unsubscribe and do-not-contact lists; CRM customer accounts and contacts; import files (all to confirm).
Who uses it: RevOps or marketing ops owns the checks; reps and marketers see why each person was flagged; CS confirms customer matches.
First version: A read-only check of all running email sequences and the last three list imports, listing everyone who declined, opted out or already buys from you, with a sample checked by hand.
How we'd measure it: People flagged before a message went out; opt-out complaints and already-a-customer replies per month, before and after.

Card text: Only talking to clients at renewal time
Problem statement: Regular check-ins don't happen, so we miss what's changed for a client until we ask them to renew.
How this agent solves it: Tracks the time since each client's last call or meeting, adds a check-in to the CSM's list when it passes a limit you set, and notes what's changed since.
Ask them about this problem: Outside renewal time, how often does each client hear from you, and who decides?
What the agent does: Gives each CSM a weekly list of clients to contact and why: unused seats, stalled setup, falling usage or a long gap since the last conversation. Each comes with a suggested question, so check-ins happen long before renewal.
How it works: Weekly, the agent reads seat logins, setup progress, usage trends and the date of each client's last call or meeting (sources to confirm) → it compares each account with its paid seats, its own recent usage and the expected setup steps → it ranks the clients worth contacting, says what changed and what's still unknown, and drafts a check-in note → the CSM edits and sends it; nothing goes out automatically.
Data it uses: Product usage and seat logins, setup milestones, CRM contacts, call and meeting dates, renewal dates (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: CS Ops owns the rules; CSMs and onboarding managers do the check-ins; the CS manager reviews who was contacted and what was learned.
First version: One CSM's accounts for a month: a weekly list with draft notes, compared with the clients that CSM would have contacted anyway.
How we'd measure it: Average days since each client's last call or meeting; seat use and setup completion after a check-in.

Card text: Happy clients. No one asks for referrals.
Problem statement: We know a client is getting good results but never ask whether they'd introduce us to someone else.
How this agent solves it: Lists clients with proven results and recent praise who haven't been asked for a referral, plus who they might introduce you to and a draft ask.
Ask them about this problem: When did you last ask a happy client for an introduction, and what happened?
What the agent does: Writes a short, sourced value story for each client from their goals, usage and own words, then spots clients with clear results who have not yet been asked for a referral.
How it works: Monthly, the agent reads each client's starting goals, usage trends, survey scores and call notes (sources to confirm) → it writes a value story that separates measured results, client quotes and estimates, and names missing proof → clients with clear results and recent positive comments go on a referral list with a suggested introduction → the CSM reviews every story and ask before anything reaches the client.
Data it uses: Stated goals from the sale, product usage, survey scores, call transcripts and emails, past referral asks (all private, access to confirm); public profiles for likely introductions.
Who uses it: CS Ops owns it; CSMs use the value story with clients and make the referral ask; marketing reviews referral and case study candidates.
First version: Value stories for 10 clients the team already sees as happy, checked by each CSM for accuracy, plus a referral list they mark yes, not yet or no.
How we'd measure it: Share of value stories CSMs would show a client as is; referral asks made and introductions received.

Card text: No one owns the client's success plan
Problem statement: Several teams work with the client, but nobody is responsible for coordinating the promised outcomes.
Roles: Customer success & accounts; Revenue & marketing ops
How this agent solves it: Turns the promised outcomes into one success plan with the CSM as coordinator and a named owner per item, then checks monthly which items are late or unowned.
Ask them about this problem: When several teams work with one client, who is responsible for the promised outcomes?
What the agent does: When a deal closes, collects everything sales promised into a sourced handoff brief, then turns it into a success plan with one named owner per outcome and a monthly check on what has slipped.
How it works: A deal is marked won in the CRM (to confirm) → the agent reads its calls, emails, proposal and order form, lists each promise with its source, and flags vague ones for the AE to clarify → it drafts a success plan with outcomes, dates and proposed owners → the AE and CSM approve it at the handoff meeting → monthly, it checks progress and tells the plan owner what has slipped.
Data it uses: CRM opportunity, call recordings and transcripts, sales emails, proposals and order forms, onboarding tasks, product usage (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: CS Ops or RevOps owns the template; the AE confirms promises; the CSM owns each success plan; onboarding, support and product leads see items assigned to them.
First version: Handoff briefs for the last 10 won deals, reviewed by each AE and CSM for missed or wrong promises before any plan is shared.
How we'd measure it: Promises found later that the brief missed; share of success plan items with a named owner and on schedule.

Card text: Client feedback never reaches the product team
Problem statement: Useful requests and complaints stay in calls and messages instead of informing product decisions.
Roles: Customer success & accounts; Support & customer experience
How this agent solves it: Pulls requests and complaints out of calls, emails and tickets into themes with counts, affected accounts and quotes, and gives product managers a monthly list for product decisions.
Ask them about this problem: How does your product team hear about client requests today, and how often?
What the agent does: Reads tickets, calls and messages to group client feedback and problems into themes, so the product team sees what clients ask for, support sees which issues keep coming back, and related tickets are treated as one problem.
How it works: Weekly, the agent reads new tickets, call transcripts, chats and survey comments (sources to confirm) → it groups items that describe the same request or problem, across clients and within one client → each theme gets a count, affected accounts, sample quotes and a likely cause marked as a guess → product and support leads review the themes; linking tickets in the help desk (to confirm) happens only after review.
Data it uses: Support tickets, call transcripts, chat and email threads, survey comments, CRM account details and renewal dates, the product team's request list (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Support Ops or CS Ops owns it; product managers review feedback themes; support leads take recurring issues to engineering; agents work grouped tickets as one case.
First version: One month of tickets and call notes grouped into themes, with a support lead and a product manager checking a sample of the groupings by hand.
How we'd measure it: Share of themes the product and support leads accept as correctly grouped; new tickets on themes marked fixed, before and after the fix.

Card text: Closed support tickets. Still-unhappy clients.
Problem statement: A ticket is marked resolved, but nobody checks whether the client feels the problem is actually fixed.
Roles: Customer success & accounts; Support & customer experience
How this agent solves it: After a ticket is marked resolved, checks the client's later replies, repeat tickets and use of the affected feature, and flags closures the client may not consider fixed.
Ask them about this problem: After a ticket closes, how would you learn the client still thinks the problem isn't fixed?
What the agent does: Reviews every account on a schedule and raises the few showing early risk, including clients the customer report shows as healthy, with the evidence behind each flag, so a CSM can act months before renewal.
How it works: Weekly, the agent reads usage trends, support tickets and replies after closure, contact changes, meeting notes and survey comments (sources to confirm) → it flags accounts whose pattern looks like past churn, including ones the customer report rates healthy, and closed tickets that look unfixed → each flag carries dated evidence, what's still unknown, a suggested owner and a first action → the CS manager reviews the list before anyone reaches out.
Data it uses: Product usage, support tickets and later replies, CRM contacts and notes, survey comments, the customer report or health scores, renewal dates (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: CS Ops owns it; CSMs act on flags; support leads follow up on closed tickets that look unfixed; RevOps and the CS leader review accuracy.
First version: Run it on last year's churned and renewed accounts to see whether it would have flagged churn earlier, including churned clients the customer report showed as healthy, before using it live.
How we'd measure it: Days of warning before churn; share of flags CSMs agree with, including those on accounts rated healthy.

Card text: Sales and CS disagree on who's ready to expand
Problem statement: Sales sees a chance to sell more while customer success sees an account that still needs work.
Roles: Customer success & accounts; Revenue & marketing ops
How this agent solves it: Shows growth signals and open problems side by side for each account, so sales and CS judge readiness from the same evidence and agree what needs fixing first.
Ask them about this problem: When sales and CS disagree about an account, who makes the call, and based on what?
What the agent does: Gives sales and customer success one shared view of which clients are ready to buy more, with the evidence for and against, a proposed owner for each opportunity and the best time to act.
How it works: Weekly, the agent reads usage against plan limits, new users and teams, open issues and risk flags (sources to confirm), plus public job posts and news → it sorts accounts into ready, not yet and blocked, with evidence on both sides and what's unknown → it proposes an owner for each opportunity from the team's agreed rules → sales and CS review the list together before anyone contacts the client.
Data it uses: Product usage and plan limits, new users by team, support tickets, risk flags, CRM opportunities and owners (to confirm); public job posts, news and leadership changes.
Who uses it: RevOps sets the rules for who acts; CSMs and account executives review the list together; the named owner acts on each opportunity.
First version: A read-only list for one team's accounts, reviewed in a joint sales and CS meeting, with both teams marking where they disagree with the agent and why.
How we'd measure it: Time from a growth signal to an agreed owner; share of ready, not yet or blocked ratings both teams accept.

Card text: Too many dupes in the CRM
Problem statement: The same person or company has several records, so activity gets split and work gets repeated.
How this agent solves it: Groups likely duplicate companies and contacts, explains each match, and proposes one surviving record, so split activity is combined once an ops owner approves the merge.
Ask them about this problem: When two records disagree, which system or field do you trust?
What the agent does: Puts likely duplicates and records with blank or inconsistent fields in a review queue, explains each flag and proposes what to keep or fix. It traces each error to the import, form or sync behind it, so the team can fix the source.
How it works: Nightly, the workflow compares records on domain, name variants, email and address, and checks required fields → it groups likely duplicates and errors with a confidence level and the reason → it proposes a surviving record or fix, and tags the import, form or sync that caused it → an ops owner approves; nothing merges automatically in version one → a weekly summary ranks error sources, each with a proposed prevention rule.
Data it uses: CRM company and contact objects, plus import, form and sync history (read access to confirm); public company domains to settle conflicts.
Who uses it: RevOps or Marketing Ops reviews the queue; the systems admin confirms merge and prevention rules; owners of each import, form or sync apply the fixes.
First version: A read-only report of the top 200 duplicate groups and the sources that created them, with a sample checked by hand for accuracy.
How we'd measure it: Duplicates found and resolved per week; hours spent on manual cleanup, before and after prevention rules go in.

Card text: New leads keep landing with the wrong rep
Problem statement: Incoming leads get assigned to people who don't cover that company, region, or type of customer.
How this agent solves it: Before assignment, it checks each lead's company, region and customer type against every rep's territory and flags any lead headed to someone who doesn't cover it.
Ask them about this problem: Which part of your territory split causes most misroutes: region, company size or customer type?
What the agent does: Checks every new lead before it reaches a rep: matches it to the right account and owner, tests the assignment against your territory rules written in plain English, and flags wrong or double ownership with the reason.
How it works: New leads arrive from forms, events or spreadsheet uploads (sources to confirm) → the workflow checks required fields, matches each lead to an existing account and owner, and fills gaps from public company data → it compares the assigned rep with the plain-English territory rules and flags mismatches and accounts with two owners → an ops owner reviews the flags; routing changes go live only after approval.
Data it uses: Lead forms and import files, CRM accounts, owners and assignment history, current routing rules and territory list (all to confirm); public company data for region and size.
Who uses it: RevOps owns the rules and reviews flags; sales managers settle ownership conflicts; reps see why each lead came to them.
First version: Run last month's leads through it read-only: rewrite the current rules in plain English, then list every lead that would have gone to a different rep and every account with two owners.
How we'd measure it: Share of leads reassigned after first routing; time from lead arrival to rep assignment; number of accounts with more than one owner.

Card text: A lead score nobody can explain
Problem statement: Leads get ranked, but nobody can tell us what makes one worth pursuing over another.
How this agent solves it: Every score lists its reasons in plain English, like company fit, the contact's role and recent pricing-page visits (to confirm), so reps see why one lead outranks another.
Ask them about this problem: Who built your current lead score, and when was it last checked against closed deals?
What the agent does: Gives every lead score a plain-English reason: which facts raised or lowered it, where each fact came from and what's still unknown, and keeps a dataset showing which scores turned into real opportunities.
How it works: A new lead arrives with its current score (to confirm) → the agent scores it against criteria written in plain English, like company fit, role and recent activity, and lists what raised or lowered it, each with its source → it notes missing data and where its view differs from the current score → the dataset records each score, its reasons and the outcome, and RevOps reviews monthly which reasons predicted real deals.
Data it uses: Lead and contact fields, the current scoring model and its inputs, marketing engagement and CRM outcomes (all to confirm); public company and role data.
Who uses it: RevOps owns the criteria and dataset; SDRs read the reasons before working a lead; sales and marketing leaders approve any change to the criteria.
First version: Score last quarter's leads both ways, with reasons shown for each, and compare which ranking better matched the leads that became opportunities, before scoring any live leads.
How we'd measure it: Opportunity rate of top-ranked leads compared with the current score; share of score reasons reps rate as accurate.

Card text: Building account lists by hand
Problem statement: Finding companies and collecting their details takes hours of manual research and spreadsheet work.
How this agent solves it: It searches public sources for companies that match the agreed criteria and collects their details into a ready list, so people review results instead of filling spreadsheets.
Ask them about this problem: What columns does your account spreadsheet have, and which take longest to fill?
What the agent does: Turns your best customers into written fit criteria, finds and scores companies that match, fills in missing company facts, and builds one ranked target list that sales and marketing both work from, with the reason behind every score.
How it works: Sales and marketing agree fit criteria, drafted from past wins and losses (to confirm) → the agent finds matching companies on the public web and fills in size, industry, location and other agreed fields → it scores each account, showing which criteria it met, missed or couldn't check, and proposes a priority tier and owner → both teams review one shared list; approved fields go back to the CRM only after sign-off (to confirm).
Data it uses: Past won and lost deals and CRM account fields (to confirm); public company websites, job posts, news and business registries for size, industry and location.
Who uses it: RevOps owns the criteria and the list; sales and marketing leaders agree priority tiers together; SDRs and AEs work the accounts while campaigns target the same list.
First version: A read-only scored list of 200 accounts, half already in the CRM with blank fields and half newly found, reviewed in one session by a sales lead and a marketing lead.
How we'd measure it: Hours spent building lists before and after; share of listed accounts both teams accept; meeting rate on top-tier accounts compared with the rest.

Card text: Copying the same data from tool to tool
Problem statement: We manually paste information between systems because updates don't carry across automatically.
Roles: Revenue & marketing ops; Systems & AI; Support & customer experience
How this agent solves it: Watches the source tool for the exact updates people now paste by hand and drafts the matching change in the destination tool, so nobody has to retype it.
Ask them about this problem: Which update do you copy by hand because the existing integration doesn't carry it across?
What the agent does: Carries updates from one tool to another so people stop pasting the same information by hand. It starts as proposed updates a person approves, then moves to automatic syncing only for fields the team has reviewed and trusts.
How it works: A change lands in the source tool, such as a deal closing or a ticket being escalated → the workflow maps the changed fields to the destination tool using the owner's approved mapping → it drafts the update with before and after values, and flags a conflict where the destination has newer data → a person approves updates in a batch, and each is logged; automatic sync is proposed per field only after review.
Data it uses: Read access to the source and destination tools, such as the CRM, support desk, billing and shared spreadsheets (to confirm); write access only after review (to confirm); the agreed field mapping.
Who uses it: RevOps or Business Systems owns the field mappings; the people who used to copy the data approve updates; system admins sign off on write access.
First version: One copy-paste task, such as closed deals into the onboarding tracker, run for two weeks as proposed updates only and compared with what people pasted by hand.
How we'd measure it: Hours spent copying data between tools, before and after; share of proposed updates approved unchanged.

How this agent solves it: Records from each system land in one case file with source links, so the reviewer works from one view and opens a system only to verify.
Ask them about this problem: Which record is hardest to get for a case, and which system holds it?
What the agent does: Builds one case file for each review from the systems involved: transactions, customer records, prior decisions and documents already received, each linked to its source, so reviewers spend their time assessing the case.
How it works: A case opens from an alert, dispute or payment review → the agent gathers the transaction, account and verification records, prior cases on the same customer or card, and documents already received (sources to confirm) → it builds a dated case file, marks missing records and pre-fills draft dispute forms from it → the reviewer checks both and submits; nothing goes to the customer or a dispute system automatically.
Data it uses: Transaction and payment records, customer account and verification records, order or delivery records, prior case notes and decisions, customer-supplied documents, dispute form templates (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Risk or payments operations owns it; reviewers and dispute analysts work from the case file; the team lead checks completeness during the pilot.
First version: Case files for 20 recently closed cases, compared with what the original reviewer gathered by hand, plus draft forms for five past disputes.
How we'd measure it: Minutes to assemble a case before and after; repeat document requests to customers on the same case.

Card text: Payment reviews pile up in a shared inbox
Problem statement: Payment cases arrive in an inbox with no reliable way to assign and track the next action.
How this agent solves it: Each inbox message becomes a tracked case with a proposed owner and next action, so the lead sees which cases are unclaimed and which are stuck.
Ask them about this problem: How do you know today which inbox cases someone has picked up?
What the agent does: Turns the shared inbox and review queues into one tracked list where every case has an owner, a next action and a deadline, ranked so urgent and near-deadline cases stand out from routine reviews.
How it works: A case arrives in the shared inbox or a review queue (to confirm) → the workflow logs its type, amount, deadline, next action and each handoff, and proposes an owner → it ranks cases by days to deadline and the urgency rules your team sets → each morning, owners and the lead get a digest of new, due-soon, overdue and unowned cases → the lead confirms owners; nothing is reassigned automatically.
Data it uses: Shared inbox and review queue messages, dispute notices and their response deadlines, payment records, team roster and assignment rules (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: The payments or risk operations lead owns it and confirms assignments; reviewers and dispute analysts work their own list; managers see overdue and unowned cases.
First version: A read-only tracker built from two weeks of shared-inbox cases, showing deadlines, proposed owners and next actions, checked by the team lead against the real queue.
How we'd measure it: Disputes that miss their evidence deadline; cases overdue or without an owner each week.

Card text: Reviewers disagree on the same kind of case
Problem statement: Similar cases receive different decisions because reviewers interpret the available evidence differently.
How this agent solves it: Monthly, the agent pairs similar cases that got different decisions and shows the evidence and reasoning side by side, so the lead can settle a shared rule.
Ask them about this problem: Which type of case gets the most inconsistent decisions between reviewers?
What the agent does: Drafts a decision record for each case at escalation and close, covering the open questions, evidence for and against, the policy version, the decision and the reasoning, which the reviewer confirms and the team can audit later.
How it works: A case is escalated or a decision is entered (to confirm) → the agent drafts the record from the case file: the questions raised and whether each is answered, evidence for and against, policy version and reasoning → the reviewer edits and confirms it, and the record is saved to the decision dataset with dated copies of the evidence → monthly, it flags similar cases with differing decisions for the team lead.
Data it uses: Case files, reviewer notes and decisions, policy versions in force at the time, reopened cases and the questions raised, record retention rules (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Risk operations owns the record format; reviewers confirm each record; team leads use it to align reviewers on similar cases; compliance or audit reads it later.
First version: Draft records for 30 closed cases, including some that were reopened, checked by a senior reviewer for missing reasoning, missing conflicting evidence and unanswered questions.
How we'd measure it: Reopened cases per month; time to reconstruct a past decision for an audit request.

Card text: Hard to explain why a transaction was flagged
Problem statement: A reviewer sees a risk alert without enough detail to understand what triggered it.
How this agent solves it: Each alert opens with the rule that fired and the exact values that tripped it, such as a new device or an unusual amount, in plain words.
Ask them about this problem: Can a reviewer see which rule fired and on which values, or only a score?
What the agent does: Explains each risk alert in plain words: which rule fired, on what values, and which evidence points to fraud or to a legitimate explanation. Likely false alarms go to a quick human check, and reviewer verdicts go back to rule owners.
How it works: A risk alert opens for review (to confirm) → the agent reads the rule that fired, the transaction and the customer's history → it explains what triggered the alert, lists evidence for and against fraud, and marks alerts with a likely legitimate explanation for a quick check → a reviewer decides and records why; nothing is cleared automatically → weekly, rule owners get a summary of alerts reviewers found wrong or unhelpful.
Data it uses: Risk alerts and the rules behind them, transaction and account history, past review outcomes, reviewer verdicts and notes (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Fraud or risk operations owns it; reviewers decide every alert; rule owners or risk analysts act on the weekly feedback.
First version: Explanations for 100 recent alerts with known outcomes, checked by two senior reviewers for accuracy and for whether the legitimate-explanation flag matched the final decision.
How we'd measure it: Time legitimate customers wait in review; share of explanations reviewers say pointed them to the right evidence.

Card text: Policy updates never reach the review checklist
Problem statement: The team keeps using an old checklist after the policy governing its decisions has changed.
How this agent solves it: When a policy changes, the workflow compares versions and drafts the matching checklist edits, so the owner approves an updated checklist instead of remembering to write one.
Ask them about this problem: After your last policy change, how long did the old checklist stay in use?
What the agent does: Keeps each review checklist matched to the current policy, attaches the right policy version to every case, and checks each case against the checklist early, so missing records surface before final review.
How it works: A policy document is updated → the workflow compares versions and drafts checklist edits → the policy owner approves them, and the new checklist is dated and linked to that policy version → as each case opens or moves stage (to confirm), the workflow attaches the policy and checklist that apply and lists required records still missing, well before final review; nothing blocks a case automatically.
Data it uses: Policy documents and their version history, current review checklists, case files and their stage, rules for which policy applies to which case type or region (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Risk policy or compliance owns the policies and approves checklist edits; risk operations runs it; reviewers see the checklist and gaps on each case.
First version: Map one policy to its checklist, show the edits the workflow would have drafted after its last change, and run the missing-record check on 20 open cases.
How we'd measure it: Days from a policy change to an updated checklist; cases reaching final review with a required record missing.

Card text: Payment records don't match across systems
Problem statement: The team must reconcile conflicting transaction details before it can finish a payment review.
How this agent solves it: Matches each transaction across payment, billing and ledger records by amount, date and reference, listing each conflicting detail and its likely cause so the payment review can finish.
Ask them about this problem: Which transaction details conflict most often, and where do you check them today?
What the agent does: Lines up each system's version of a disputed number, record or transaction, explains the likely reason they differ, and shows which value looks current. Settled answers build a shared list of which system and definition to trust for each number and field.
How it works: Someone flags a disputed number, record or payment, or a scheduled check finds one → the workflow pulls that item from each system → it compares them field by field and names each gap's likely cause: definitions, timing, filters or entry errors → it shows the likely current value, with update times and what's still unknown → the owner confirms and the answer joins the trusted-source list; nothing is corrected automatically in version one.
Data it uses: Records and change history from the CRM, billing, finance reports, dashboards and payment systems; written metric definitions where they exist (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: RevOps or Business Systems owns it; finance or payment operations reviews payment cases; the owner of each metric or system makes the final call.
First version: One disputed metric, such as last quarter's closed revenue, reconciled across two systems, plus 20 recent mismatched records or payments, with each explanation checked by its owner.
How we'd measure it: Time from spotting a mismatch to an agreed answer; share of explanations the system owner confirms as correct.

Card text: Fraud patterns are spotted one case too late
Problem statement: The team sees a recurring pattern only after several related cases have already been handled.
How this agent solves it: Each new case is checked against open and recent ones, so cases sharing a device or address are linked from the second case, whoever reviewed the first.
Ask them about this problem: How do reviewers share a suspicion that a case looks like one they saw earlier?

How it works: Daily, the agent reads new, open and recently closed cases (to confirm) → it groups cases that share details such as a device, address, email pattern or card range, or that follow the same sequence of events → it writes a pattern note: the linked cases, what they share, what is inferred and what is still unknown → the fraud lead confirms the pattern before reviewers are alerted or any rule changes.
Data it uses: Case records and outcomes, transaction details, device, address and account identifiers, reviewer notes (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: The fraud lead owns it and confirms each pattern; reviewers get confirmed pattern notes on matching open cases; rule owners decide on rule changes.
First version: Run it on last quarter's cases and check whether it would have linked the patterns your team found by hand, and how many cases sooner.
How we'd measure it: Cases handled before a pattern was flagged, compared with past patterns; share of pattern notes the fraud lead confirms.

Card text: The case summary leaves out conflicting evidence
Problem statement: A summary presents one conclusion without showing the records that point to a different interpretation.
How this agent solves it: The record has a required section for evidence pointing the other way, which the agent fills from the case file or marks as none found.
Ask them about this problem: When evidence conflicts on a case, where does your team record the side that lost?
What the agent does: Drafts a decision record for each case at escalation and close, covering the open questions, evidence for and against, the policy version, the decision and the reasoning, which the reviewer confirms and the team can audit later.
How it works: A case is escalated or a decision is entered (to confirm) → the agent drafts the record from the case file: the questions raised and whether each is answered, evidence for and against, policy version and reasoning → the reviewer edits and confirms it, and the record is saved to the decision dataset with dated copies of the evidence → monthly, it flags similar cases with differing decisions for the team lead.
Data it uses: Case files, reviewer notes and decisions, policy versions in force at the time, reopened cases and the questions raised, record retention rules (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Risk operations owns the record format; reviewers confirm each record; team leads use it to align reviewers on similar cases; compliance or audit reads it later.
First version: Draft records for 30 closed cases, including some that were reopened, checked by a senior reviewer for missing reasoning, missing conflicting evidence and unanswered questions.
How we'd measure it: Reopened cases per month; time to reconstruct a past decision for an audit request.

Card text: Asking customers twice for the same evidence
Problem statement: Different reviewers request documents that the customer has already supplied for the same case.
How this agent solves it: The case file lists every document the customer already supplied, with date and channel, so any new request covers only what is still missing.
Ask them about this problem: Where do customer-supplied documents land today, and can every reviewer see them?
What the agent does: Builds one case file for each review from the systems involved: transactions, customer records, prior decisions and documents already received, each linked to its source, so reviewers spend their time assessing the case.
How it works: A case opens from an alert, dispute or payment review → the agent gathers the transaction, account and verification records, prior cases on the same customer or card, and documents already received (sources to confirm) → it builds a dated case file, marks missing records and pre-fills draft dispute forms from it → the reviewer checks both and submits; nothing goes to the customer or a dispute system automatically.
Data it uses: Transaction and payment records, customer account and verification records, order or delivery records, prior case notes and decisions, customer-supplied documents, dispute form templates (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Risk or payments operations owns it; reviewers and dispute analysts work from the case file; the team lead checks completeness during the pilot.
First version: Case files for 20 recently closed cases, compared with what the original reviewer gathered by hand, plus draft forms for five past disputes.
How we'd measure it: Minutes to assemble a case before and after; repeat document requests to customers on the same case.

Card text: No feedback when a risk alert was wrong
Problem statement: The people maintaining our review rules do not hear which alerts reviewers found unhelpful or incorrect.
How this agent solves it: Reviewers mark each alert as useful, wrong or unhelpful with a reason, and rule owners get a weekly summary by rule with example cases.
Ask them about this problem: How do the people who write your rules hear what reviewers think of them?
What the agent does: Explains each risk alert in plain words: which rule fired, on what values, and which evidence points to fraud or to a legitimate explanation. Likely false alarms go to a quick human check, and reviewer verdicts go back to rule owners.
How it works: A risk alert opens for review (to confirm) → the agent reads the rule that fired, the transaction and the customer's history → it explains what triggered the alert, lists evidence for and against fraud, and marks alerts with a likely legitimate explanation for a quick check → a reviewer decides and records why; nothing is cleared automatically → weekly, rule owners get a summary of alerts reviewers found wrong or unhelpful.
Data it uses: Risk alerts and the rules behind them, transaction and account history, past review outcomes, reviewer verdicts and notes (all private, access to confirm).
Who uses it: Fraud or risk operations owns it; reviewers decide every alert; rule owners or risk analysts act on the weekly feedback.
First version: Explanations for 100 recent alerts with known outcomes, checked by two senior reviewers for accuracy and for whether the legitimate-explanation flag matched the final decision.
How we'd measure it: Time legitimate customers wait in review; share of explanations reviewers say pointed them to the right evidence.
